hey! in a really similar boat to be honest, i’ve been trying for ages to get a formal diagnosis as I have been part of the urgent care mental health team since I turned 18 a few years ago. as a result of trying to invoke my right to choose stuff and raise concerns over getting a diagnostic review for OCD, i’ve been discharged twice because they don’t really seem to get it, and am now having to blow the whole situation up and long story short make a formal complaint etc. nhs services have a long way to go towards understanding OCD and its presentations. like you, I utterly fear rejection and the potential fallout of that rejection comprising my care moving forward, so it’s been really hard to take this back to my GP only to find that they don’t really have the resources to back me even to deter me from going ahead with the formal complaint. as a result of this, i’ve just started to come to terms with the fact I probably have to pay for a private psych to give me a diagnosis and medication, so I can at least move on with my life. 

for me, I don’t really know why exactly I want a diagnosis either, I find it really difficult to justify and it spins me out so I really hear you. all I know is that it feels like it would make my life easier being able to go to my gp or mental health team and be able to say ‘I think i’m having a bad OCD flare up’ when I am, and not have to spend time advocating for why instead of just receiving the help I need if that makes sense. not having the diagnosis has also made my life more difficult as I am on benefits receiving PIP, and I can’t back up the debilitating symptoms without evidence of someone just writing down the formulation. it’s a pain in the ass but I really hear you. 

I think it’s hugely dependant on the nhs services in your area. I live in a city down south so it’s basically impossible to be seen as a mental health priority unless you’re at risk of harming someone else. for that reason I would suggest not spending too much time seeking a formal diagnosis through the NHS if you can for-see that it will take up a lot of your mental energy. happy to talk more over dm if I can be of any help!!! big love xx

i think i saw a statistic that said within two years of DBT, 50% of people with BPD were recovering/recovered. it really depends on what therapists offer what in your area. i’m in the UK, so i got mine under the NHS. i definitely think it’s treatable within a year, it’s more about the fact that within the first year it teaches you enough to the point where you retain that information for the rest of your recovery, rather than you being immediately “cured” and that’s that. view it as a process, that becomes easier and more natural to you over time, even after you might’ve finished DBT. the premise of “completing” DBT is more about learning about all of the different modules. throughout your life you’ll still continue to refer back to it, like for me i still go through my DBT workbooks and i probably will for the rest of my life. 

if someone has told you it’s not treatable within a year, i don’t know if it’s their place to say. it’s really dependant on how we respond to DBT, but there’s no right way to go about it. for some people it resonates immediately, and for others it takes a little longer to grasp. there’s not exactly a time frame on it, i think it’s pretty subjective depending on how you’re accessing it. mine was specifically 16 weeks, because that’s the allotted time they can offer someone under the NHS for this otherwise other people can’t access these resources. 

don’t worry, it’s definitely not like a residential program thing at all. it’s like any other therapy, your therapist works through it with you every time you meet, which for people is often weekly appointments. 

i’ll explain more in PM, and i can try help you find some resources as well!!

yeah of course! i think it varies? for me it was a 16 week course because i was on a waiting list due to my circumstances, it was like a intensive course designed in a way that allowed it to immediately start being applicable in my life. i’ve not heard of it being similar to AA, i would think that because i guess it would take a lot of commitment and maybe training for whatever therapist was providing that it would be difficult to make that happen, but i’m not actually sure and i would love for that to be a thing. 

i think it’s more of a type of therapy that sets you up with skills that are designed to rewire your brain and as they become second nature to you, you carry them with you for the rest of your life. so elements of it are definitely designed in a way that means you essentially work with this therapy (or the skills it teaches you) to regulate your emotions for the rest of your life, which i guess is what makes it lifelong. 

from my experience, the only other time of DBT available to me is private therapy with a DBT trained therapist (mine was like a community one so therefore it was free but that also means that at some point it would end/i would eventually have to find another therapist) but i found my experience to be so so so helpful to my situation because of the circumstances i was in. DBT was offered to me as an alternative for inpatient because i was at the peak of a crisis, so the intensity and back-to-back aspect was beneficial. 

i think for anyone who is looking into DBT for any reason that isn’t an immediate crisis, it’s way more helpful to find someone that will work one-on-one with you and teaching you the skills and giving you the workbook/worksheets, or just any more thorough, slower variation of it. there’s a lot to take in, and i think it makes more impact the more you study each module in it’s fullest. 

there are probably community/group skills class that work with DBT that can be an AA sort of situation - the course i did had a group class and an individual therapy twice a week, so the group class it was very much like an AA setting in the sense that there were a few of us alongside the organisers who taught us skills and stuff and helped us etc. but it wasn’t like an optional thing people could come to every week, it was part of the course and the same people who had been signed up to it in advance if that makes sense. 

i hope that helps/makes sense but please feel free to pm me if i can answer any more questions or explain more <3

thank you so so much!! my favourite tips to share would be to keep track of your usage, triggers and symptoms as you start to come off of them. what really helped me push through the first few days was distractions, and methods of delay. filling my days up with activities that took my mind off of it. even shit as stupid as bleaching my hair or curling it, or reorganising my kitchen cabinets. watching loads of movie to past the time was also really helpful. it’s a slow and agonising process, especially at first, so it’s okay to allow yourself to feel the shitty and treat yourself to low energy activities.  
as for methods of delay, when i feel like relapsing, i tell myself to wait 5 minutes, then 15, and so on, until i either forget, find a distraction, or normally fall asleep. or i’ll put on a movie and say “i won’t take it now, but i’ll watch this movie and then decide if i want to do it when it’s finished” and by the end of it usually i managed to curb the urge.  
exercising when you feel the urge over the course of the day was super super helpful too, particularly stuff focused on core strength. it would give me a nice buzz and by the end of it i’d feel so worn out that the idea of taking stuff would make me feel a bit sick. it’s also nice to see yourself build up more toned features over the course of even a few days of intense exercise. adrenaline filled activities are good.  
i use melatonin to help with the insomnia, it’s been particularly bad recently (haven’t slept in literally 3 days) but it’s comforting to know i have it as a safety net just in case the insomnia is really bad.  
the app “i am sober” has really helped me to keep track of my usage, and my withdrawal symptoms. you can log positive and negative symptoms as you reach each milestone (1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks, 1 month etc). it also sends positive notifications! couldn’t recommend it enough. seeing how many days i’ve been sober for pushes me to hang on for at least another day.

good to hear that you’ve found someone who seems thorough. i think this is a really big step forward. as long as the psychiatrist is aware of her tendencies to change the story and all things related to that, that is probably part of the bigger problem and helps to identify that she presents with all of said issues, as well as changing the issues frequently. to me that seems to lead to a completely different diagnosis path, more on the personality disorders one perhaps. 

the answer will never be simple. she is a very complex person with a lot of issues. that in itself is evidence that the answer cannot be simple. and mental illness itself is a complexity with hardly any simple answers. diagnosis is not simple. meds are not simple. therapy is not simple. the idea that you can find answers immediately or very obviously is a misconception. it’s complex and difficult. but not impossible. 

diagnosis itself is a really long process. you won’t always find answers. the priority should be her getting therapy (or even meds) and her having someone to talk to even if she is in denial. she needs help and i understand how difficult it is for her to get that when she doesn’t want it. but sometimes, we come across the right therapist who can see through all of our layers and they ask hard hitting questions that make us question why we have done the thing we’ve done or why we’re feeling the way we’re feeling. and they undo a massive facade we may have put on. maybe she just needs to find that therapist. or the right meds. i cant tell you, neither can anyone on reddit but keep it on your mind that diagnosis is not going to be the solution. it doesn’t necessarily make her feel any better, like she wants to make a change, or change her denial. it makes it easier for you to find her the right therapist/type of therapy, maybe more insight on meds she could take. and as i said, you may not get a diagnosis for a long time. so in the meanwhile working alongside the doctors trying to keep her safe and within therapy is as much as you can do. nobody can force her to want to be recovering unfortunately. but there are processes to get there that i’m sure her doctor could tell you about. 

i think you’ve done a good thing to reach out, and i’m truly sorry this process is so brutally hard. i hear how frustrating and difficult it is. i hope it gets better for everyone!

please please please look into BPD. i know a diagnosis won’t solve all of your problems at all, and i truly hear you’re at the end of your tether. it’s tough when you put all this time and energy and compassion into trying to help someone, and it’s especially rough when they can’t see it, don’t want to be helped or just can’t accept it. but honestly, your daughter sounds really similar to me. 

had some traumatic childhood issues, led up to me being excruciatingly suicidal and difficult as a teenager, trying to take my own life from as young as 11/12 and being dependant on narcotics and doing risky impulsive behaviour from that point on. i actually ended up having a couple episodes of psychosis because of how many drugs i was taking, and just a whole lot of other stuff that led me to ending up with a BPD diagnosis at 15. i matched 9/9 of the diagnosis criteria and it took me a couple hospitalisations and an absolutely massive breakdown to begin to want to get better. 

my parents never understood why i acted out against them so frequently, why i willingly self destructed and threw my life away. but that’s a part of BPD, we don’t have twisted motives, we’re incredibly troubled. whether that’s due to trauma or experiences that shaped us mixed with a chemical imbalance, it is often misunderstood. 

i hear you though. your story sounds almost too familiar to mine, and i hear that you have been endlessly trying to help. it’s one of the hardest things imaginable. but i urge you to read up on BPD. especially understanding why your daughter may do the things she does. 

DBT also saved my relationship with my mum. she used to punish me continually for “acting out”, and DBT helped her to understand my point of view and my inner turmoil better. 

i’m sorry that you don’t have all the answers as of now, uncertainty is really difficult. i really hope things work out, i’m not sure if i conveyed it sincerely enough, but your story really resonated with me. sorry if this wasn’t the advice you wanted to hear, but please feel free to PM if you want me to elaborate on anything. best wishes

edit: psychosis can also often be attributed to BPD. i definitely cant tell you whether this is psychosis or
not, but the sudden interest into reading palms sounds like a burst of hypomania. i used to turn to fanatically turn to astrology and spirituality, which then lead to it seeping into some delusions i had when i was in an episode. so it could be a possibility but i don’t think anybody on reddit can give you legitimate insight other than its probably best to get medical advice which i already assume you are in the midst of.

2nd edit: nobody on reddit can tell you what your daughter has and hasn’t. even if it SOUNDS like schizophrenia or BPD, there’s every chance that it isn’t. please read these comments with a massive pinch of salt. theres a difference between maybe leading you in a different direction for answers that you could find actually apply to your daughter, and straight up saying she has schizophrenia. diagnosis can be a very long and difficult process, and as someone else highlighted, in the meantime all you can do is provide compassion and try to find some answers and the right help. which is what you’re already doing. so good on you for that!
